title: Gas at a damaged house, and when the supply fails
summary: A gas smell means switch nothing and get out; shut the gas off from outside at the meter or tank valve. Don't trust your nose alone: the smell can fade. When the supply fails, close every appliance valve so nothing leaks when pressure comes back. Leak-testing with soapy water is your job; opening joints, reconnecting and relighting a whole house is a gas fitter's.

materials.item: Adjustable wrench at least 30 cm (12 in) long, kept near the meter
Spray bottle or brush, with water and a little chloride-free soap (or a gas leak-detector solution)
Tape and a marker for tags

steps.text: Smell gas (rotten eggs, or boiled cabbage for propane), hear hissing, or a gas detector sounds: stop. Switch nothing on or off: no lights, phone, lighter, match or appliance (BC gas brochure, PERC safety guide, TSASK propane).
steps.warn: A switch, phone or appliance can make the spark that sets it off. Treat a detector alarm as a leak even if you smell nothing (PERC safety guide).

steps.text: Get everyone out. Leave the door open behind you and any windows that are already open (BC gas brochure). Don't go back in for anything. Once you are well away, and if a phone works, call 911 and the gas company's emergency line (BC gas brochure). Stay out until an official or the gas company says it is safe (BC gas brochure, PERC safety guide).

From outside, shut off natural gas at the valve on the inlet pipe beside the meter (BC gas brochure). Turn it a quarter turn either way, so the handle crosses the pipe (PG&E outages, WA EMD). Use a wrench at least 30 cm (12 in) long (WA EMD). If the meter or its valve is inside the building, don't go in for it (PERC: never enter an area if you suspect a gas leak).
steps.warn: Don't spray WD-40 on a valve rusted open: it can damage the seals (WA EMD). Don't hammer it. If the leak is at the meter or the valve itself, leave it and stay away.

steps.text: Propane: close the main valve on the tank by turning it right (clockwise), unless you think the leak is at the tank itself (PERC safety guide). For a small cylinder, close its valve the same way.

At a damaged or abandoned house, stop at the doorway and smell before you go in, and don't enter if you smell gas or a detector sounds (PERC safety guide). Look at the meter, the pipes where they enter, and the propane tank: a shifted tank or bent, broken or damaged gas lines means close the main valve first (PERC safety guide).
steps.warn: Propane is heavier than air and settles in basements and low spots (Goodman IO-359J). Sniff low as well as high. A detector beats your nose.

steps.text: Don't trust smell alone. The odorant can fade in soil, concrete, building materials, rust and water, and a nose dulled by a cold or long exposure misses it (NIOSH odor fade, PERC safety guide). Use a combustible gas detector if you have one (NIOSH odor fade).
Leak-test with bubbles, never a flame. With the gas on and the appliance off, brush or spray soapy water on each joint you are checking. Bubbles forming mean a leak (Goodman IO-359J, TSASK propane).
steps.warn: Use chloride-free soap or a leak-detector solution, and rinse it off afterwards: kitchen detergents can corrode gas piping (Lennox 1120, Goodman IO-359J).

steps.text: Leak at a propane cylinder's hose or regulator connection: close the cylinder valve, tighten that connection, and test again. If it still bubbles, close the valve and leave it closed (PERC safety guide, TSASK propane). A cylinder hissing at its own valve: close the valve if there is no flame or visible cloud, keep it upright so it can't fall or roll, and leave the area (PERC safety guide).
steps.warn: Never move or carry a leaking cylinder in a vehicle (PERC safety guide). Leaking propane can freeze skin (PERC safety guide).

steps.text: Leak anywhere on the house piping, a meter, or a joint at an appliance: shut the gas off at the meter or tank and leave it off. Tag the valve: "Gas leak. Off. Do not open."
steps.warn: Don't undo, tighten or take apart house gas joints or appliance valves. An open gas line leaks (PERC safety guide).

steps.text: When the supply fails or runs out, go round every gas appliance: turn its own shut-off valve off (handle across the pipe), set pilot knobs to OFF, and turn every range knob to OFF. For propane, then close the tank valve (turn it right). For natural gas, utilities ask you to close the meter only for a leak or damage, because a closed meter can delay restoration (PG&E outages, Enbridge outage); with no utility working that is your call.
steps.warn: A valve left open when the gas runs out can leak when the system is filled again (Superior Propane, Eastern Propane). Range burners left at LITE pour gas into the room (GE outage).

steps.text: Relight a pilot only by the lighting instructions on that appliance's label, and not if you smell gas (PERC safety guide). If it went out, wait 5 minutes or more with the knob at OFF first, and stop if you then smell gas (NRCan gas fireplaces, Travis 864 ST). Enbridge Gas tells its customers to hire a contractor for this (Enbridge outage).
steps.warn: If a pilot is hard to light or keeps going out, leave it off. Don't bleed air from a gas line: you release gas (PERC safety guide).

steps.text: Never use a gas appliance that has been under water. Lennox (for its furnace) and Travis (for its fireplace) say to have every gas control and any control part that got wet replaced before it is used again (Lennox EL297UHV, Travis 864 ST).
steps.warn: Leave a flooded appliance shut off at its own valve, and tag it.

steps.text: Fit CO alarms with battery backup on every level and outside every sleeping area (Health Canada CO, BC gas brochure), and keep every appliance vent and the meter clear of snow, by hand or with a broom (BC gas brochure, PERC safety guide).

notes:
## Why gas goes wrong after a disaster

Gas leaks and explosions cause many of the fires after a big earthquake (WA EMD). Floods, snow and ice damage gas equipment, storms shift tanks and bend lines (PERC safety guide), and collapsing buildings break pipes. Then nobody comes to fix them. A smell, a hiss or a meter dial spinning faster than normal are all warning signs (WA EMD).

## Natural gas and propane

| | Natural gas | Propane |
|---|---|---|
| Comes from | A utility pipe, through a meter and regulator | A tank or cylinder outside the house |
| Smell | Mercaptan added: rotten eggs or sulphur (BC gas brochure) | An odorant added: like boiled cabbage (TSASK propane) |
| What it is | Mostly methane (BC gas brochure) | Propane: heavier than air, so a leak settles in basements and low spots (Goodman IO-359J) |
| Main shut-off | Valve on the inlet pipe beside the meter (BC gas brochure) | Main valve on the tank: right (clockwise) to close (PERC safety guide) |

Appliances are built for one gas or the other and say which on the rating plate (Travis 864 ST). Some natural gas appliances can be converted to propane, by a qualified person (PERC safety guide), with the maker's conversion kit (Travis 864 ST).

## Shutting off

- Natural gas: a quarter turn either way so the valve's handle crosses the pipe (PG&E outages; WA EMD). Open, it lines up with the pipe. Keep a 30 cm (12 in) wrench by the meter (WA EMD).
- Shut it off when you smell gas, hear hissing or see the meter dial spinning fast (WA EMD). Utilities ask you not to close the meter without a reason: PG&E says a closed valve can delay restoration, and Enbridge Gas says only it or emergency crews should close a meter, apart from the leak, damage and fire conditions it lists for earthquakes (PG&E outages; Enbridge outage). Turning it back on needs them or a licensed contractor (BC gas brochure; FortisBC earthquake). With no utility left, a leak matters far more than that.
- Each appliance also has its own shut-off valve on its gas pipe (PG&E outages). Closing that is enough when only one appliance is the problem.
- If an appliance overheats or its gas won't shut off, close its manual gas valve before you cut its power (Lennox EL297UHV).

## Leak testing

Makers say to check gas joints with chloride-free soap and water, a leak-detector solution or an electronic gas detector, and never a match or open flame (Goodman IO-359J). Lennox warns that kitchen detergents can corrode the metals in gas piping and that some leak-test soaps are corrosive, so rinse the piping after the test (Lennox 1120). For a cylinder: put leak-detector solution or thick soapy water on the whole valve area and connection, open the cylinder valve slowly and watch for bubbles; if they appear, close the valve, tighten the connection and test again; if they still appear, close the valve and leave it (PERC safety guide). Do it each time you connect a cylinder (PERC safety guide).

An electronic detector finds leaks you can't smell. The propane industry says to install propane detectors and to act on an alarm even with no smell (PERC safety guide).

## Odorant fade

The smell is added. It can fade or vanish. NIOSH warns firefighters not to rely on smell, because gas that passes through soil, concrete, drywall, wood or new pipe and tanks can lose its odour (NIOSH odor fade). Rust in a propane tank cuts the odorant (Goodman IO-359J). Air and moisture get into a tank that ran empty and cause rust that weakens the smell (Superior Propane). A cold, age, sleep, other strong smells and simply getting used to it all dull your nose (PERC safety guide).

## When the supply fails

When a propane tank runs dry, every pilot goes out (Superior Propane; Eastern Propane), and a natural gas outage does the same: Manitoba Hydro says you may need to relight furnace and water heater pilots when gas is restored (Manitoba Hydro winter). If any appliance valve is left open, gas leaks out of it when the pressure returns (Eastern Propane). That is why you close every appliance valve and set every control to OFF first. The industry rule is that a qualified person leak-tests the system before gas is turned back on, and never the owner at the tank (PERC safety guide; Eastern Propane).

## Relighting a house and reconnecting: a fitter's job, and why

FortisBC and the BC government say only a licensed gas contractor or technician can safely turn gas back on at a meter (FortisBC earthquake; BC gas brochure). Utilities that restore service go house to house, turn the meter on and relight every appliance (FortisBC earthquake). Enbridge Gas wants a technician in the home and an adult present, and tells customers not to restore service or relight appliances themselves (Enbridge outage). Manitoba Hydro relights appliances it shut off for safety, and says that if you relight them yourself you should follow the instructions on your equipment (Manitoba Hydro meters). The risks they are managing:
- An appliance valve or range knob left open fills the house when gas comes back.
- A pipe broken out of sight, or a joint that moved, leaks into a wall or crawl space.
- An appliance was removed and its pipe left open. A disconnected appliance's line must be capped or plugged by someone qualified (PERC safety guide).
- A vent is blocked by snow, ice or a nest (PERC safety guide), or by a collapsed chimney, and the appliance fills the house with CO.
- An appliance that was under water still has its wet gas controls, which Lennox says must be replaced (Lennox EL297UHV).
- A pilot that won't light tempts people to bleed air from the line, which releases gas (PERC safety guide).

Never open a gas joint, remove a gas valve or move an appliance on its connector yourself (PERC safety guide). For taking parts from a furnace, see [Furnace teardown](#guides/teardown_furnace).

## When no help is coming

**Leaks**
- Gas off at the meter or tank, tagged, and leave it off. A house with a leak you can't find is not worth the risk. Heat one room another way: see [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm).
- Air the house only from outside: open doors and windows you can reach without going in, then stay out. A gone smell is not an all-clear, because odorant can fade (NIOSH odor fade; PERC safety guide): go back in only with a combustible gas detector that reads clear, and keep switches, lighters and flames out of the house until then. If the smell comes back, leave the gas off for good.
- A cylinder that won't stop leaking at its valve: if there is no flame or cloud, close the valve, keep it upright and leave the area (PERC safety guide). Don't put it in a vehicle (PERC safety guide).

**Bringing gas back**

No utility or propane source gives an owner a method for opening the gas to a house system, so this card doesn't either. FortisBC and the BC government say only a licensed gas contractor can turn gas on safely at a meter (FortisBC earthquake; BC gas brochure). Enbridge Gas tells customers not to restore service or relight appliances themselves (Enbridge outage). PERC says never to turn the gas on at the propane tank yourself, because a qualified person must leak-check the system first (PERC safety guide). What you can do yourself:
1. Leave the meter or tank valve as it is, with every appliance valve closed and every control at OFF. If the utility is still working, it turns the meter on and relights appliances house to house (FortisBC earthquake).
2. If the supply returns on its own (the meter was never closed), smell around each appliance, low down as well, before you light anything, and stop if there is any gas smell (Lennox EL297UHV). Soap-test the joints you can reach (Goodman IO-359J) and rinse afterwards (Lennox 1120). Relight a pilot only by the appliance's label (PERC safety guide). A pilot that won't stay lit, or soot, means shut it off and leave it (PERC safety guide).
3. A portable propane cylinder is not a house system: you connect it, bubble-test it and open its valve slowly yourself, outdoors, as above (PERC safety guide).
4. Anyone with a headache or dizziness: everyone out (see [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)). Heat one room another way: see [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm).

To know which gas appliances work with no electricity, see [Gas without power](#guides/reference_gas_without_power).
